name: IS1009c
method: keypoints = AMI abstractive annotation (decisions, actions, problems, abstract sentences) mapped to keyword groups and spans by Claude (Opus); questions written by Claude from the gold transcript

keypoints.text: The interface specialist begins her presentation by highlighting important remote functions and showing examples of remote interfaces.
She talks about the technical electronic components of the remote, explains how a remote works, and shows a few pictures revealing the insides of a normal remote control.
She suggests giving the remote a strong shell so it is durable.
She suggests using a rechargeable battery.
She suggests not adding a scroll wheel because it requires a sophisticated chip.
The marketing expert presents, talking about user preferences for a small, simple, eye-catching, cute, appealing, and functional remote.
Fruit and vegetable shapes are popular this year, so a soft, spongy remote perhaps covered with cloth could make the item marketable.
The group discusses the issues surrounding speech recognition, noting that if it is good quality it could be costly.
They decided that the product should be bright, colorful, trendy in design, strong, and compact.
They decided that the product should have push buttons.
They decided the product should contain supplement features (possibly mute button, swapping button, voice recognition).
The power source will be batteries because it is cost-effective.
They will have the industrial engineer do more research on the cost of voice recognition before deciding whether to include that function.
The group would like to include voice recognition as a feature, but they are not sure about how much it would cost.
This will require further research by the industrial engineer.
The marketing expert will do the product evaluation.
The industrial designer and interface specialist will work together on a prototype using modeling clay.
The industrial designer will come up with a user interface design.
Their coaches will send specific instructions and answer questions.

questions.q: In the remote control design meeting, what situation did the interface designer give to explain why a mute button is useful?
questions.answer: When the viewer gets a telephone call, they can bring the sound down without switching off the TV and keep watching.

questions.q: In the remote control design meeting, what example did the interface designer use for the subtitles button?
questions.answer: Watching a French program and wanting English subtitles.

questions.q: In the remote control design meeting, how many pins did the chip inside the opened-up remote have?
In the remote control design meeting, why did the industrial designer say the circuit board is cheap to build?
questions.answer: It is just printed rather than wired, the prints act as wires and circuits, and boards can be built in bulk.

questions.q: In the remote control design meeting, what outdoor temperatures did the industrial designer say the integrated circuit should withstand?
questions.answer: High temperatures like thirty-eight or forty degrees, as well as low temperatures.

questions.q: In the remote control design meeting, how did the marketing expert research what the competition was doing?
questions.answer: By looking at press and ads for other remotes, surfing the internet, and noticing and asking about remotes in people's houses.

questions.q: In the remote control design meeting, what example did the interface designer give of using the voice recognition feature in the morning?
questions.answer: Saying a prerecorded 'good morning' at around eight o'clock makes the TV recognise her voice and switch on to the news.
